title: Chase Software Bug Knocked Out Banking for Millions on Monday — and It Wasn’t a Cyberattack
excerpt: A software bug in JPMorgan Chase’s systems slowed banking nationwide Monday, delaying Zelle payments and transfers. Chase says service is back to normal — and it was not a cyberattack.
content:
A software bug inside JPMorgan Chase’s own systems slowed banking across the United States on Monday, November 16, delaying transactions, Zelle payments and balance checks for customers at Chase and several other major banks. By Monday evening, Chase said transactions were posting normally again.

Chase told USA TODAY the problem was a “software bug” in its on-premise hardware systems and was “not cyber related.” The bank said customers kept access to their accounts and funds, but some transactions took longer than usual to complete.

Reports of problems surged through the afternoon on Downdetector, the outage-tracking site. Chase reports peaked at about 4,800 around 2 p.m. Eastern time — the bank’s second-highest number of reports in a 15-minute window in at least a year, according to Downdetector’s parent company, Ookla. Reports also spiked for Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One and Zelle.

Bank of America and U.S. Bank each told USA TODAY their own systems were not directly affected. U.S. Bank said customers trying to move money to or from “another financial institution” through Zelle could see delays, and Bank of America suggested customers with delays contact the other provider directly. Zelle said its own platform was operating “as it should,” noting that consumers use Zelle through their banks, which hold the funds.

There is no evidence the outage was a cyberattack. Chase said so in its statement, an FBI official told FOX Business there was no indication of outside cyber activity, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday night that investigators had found no proof of a cyberattack. Mullin suggested the failures may be tied to artificial intelligence being built into existing digital infrastructure — his assessment, not a finding by investigators.

The banking disruption was the third major technology failure in five days, following a Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and Microsoft 365 services and a nationwide FAA ground stop that halted flights. Analysts quoted by USA TODAY said the run of failures shows how concentrated critical systems have become: “When one piece fails, it fails at national scale,” said Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy.

What to do if your payment was delayed

Do not resubmit a transfer or Zelle payment that froze mid-process — duplicate attempts can result in duplicate charges once systems recover. Save screenshots of error messages and timestamps, in case a delayed payment causes a missed bill or an overdraft fee you need to dispute. And beware of phishing: scammers exploit big outages with urgent texts and emails claiming an account is locked. Do not click links in unsolicited messages.

For Laredo readers who bank with Chase or send money through Zelle, the practical takeaway is the same: check that any payment sent Monday actually posted, and check with the other party before sending it again.

Chase has not said how many customers were affected or what exactly went wrong in the software release. Webb Watch 956 will update this story if the bank releases more detail.

Source: USA TODAY, Nov. 16, 2026; Reuters, Nov. 16, 2026.
